newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean parties set fresh deadline for labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean parties set fresh deadline for labour law.

text.p: South Korean lawmakers on Friday failed to agree on a new labour law to replace one that sparked almost a month of costly strikes, but gave themselves another week to strike a deal.

The failure to reach a compromise during two weeks of heated wrangling means the controversial bill that was rammed through Parliament on December 26 will now take effect on Saturday in its original form -- but will not be enforced.
The ruling New Korea Party and two opposition groups had wanted to agree on a blueprint by Friday, but now have extended that deadline until March 8.

President Kim Young-sam was forced to return the legislation to parliament for revision. Its passage at a dawn session of the National Assembly at which the opposition was not present sparked worker fury and fierce opposition at home and abroad.
"We apologise to the people that we have not forged a single final proposal due to differences on several sticking points," the parties said in a statement.
The New Korea Party, the main opposition National Congress for New Politics and the United Liberal Democratic Party control 280 seats in the 299-member parliament.

A parliamentary committee agreed earlier on Friday to water down key provisions of the law. This included a two-year delay in implementing a controversial clause that would allow companies to lay off workers.
Worker layoffs are virtually unheard of in South Korea, where companies guarantee jobs for life.
It also agreed to immediately recognise an outlawed union body that organised strikes that cost South Korea $3.28 billion in lost production and $509 million in lost exports.

The panel was deadlocked on several thorny provisions, including articles making it illegal for companies to pay wages to workers for the time they are on strike, and barring them from paying full-time union organisers from 2002.
The issue of layoffs and free labour union association aroused the greatest passions among opponents of the law.
Employers argued the new law was needed to bring down costs and make South Korean industry more competitive.
In principle, the committee agreed to the introduction of flexible working hours -- a clause demanded by employers -- but was unable to fix the maximum length of the working day.

It weakened a provision that allowed companies to replace strikers with outside workers, agreeing only that replacements must be from within the company and allowing companies to sub-contract production.
The government said the new law was desperately needed to give companies flexibility.
The outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions had called on Thursday for a half-day strike on Friday, but the response from workers was lukewarm.
Public transport and hospitals were not affected.

In an informal survey of about 20 companies under the confederation's umbrella, only two reported work disruptions -- Hyundai Motor Co and Daewoo Motors, which were at the forefront of strkes earlier this year.
A Daewoo Motor spokesman said only 30 percent of union workers downed tools for four hours.
The confederation said in a statement that it could no longer rely on politicians, and threatened unspecified "strong action" to press for worker demands.
